newsitem.title: BELGIUM: BRUSSELS' HUB ROLE ATTRACTS SONY, WESTERN UNION.
newsitem.headline: BRUSSELS' HUB ROLE ATTRACTS SONY, WESTERN UNION.

text.p: The Belgian capital's geographic location at the heart of western Europe, and its central role in European Union politics, together with a favourable tax regime, are earning it dozens of new jobs.

Japanese electronics giant Sony Corp and U.S. electronic financial services group Western Union are close to setting up businesses in Brussels, spokesman Eric Van Coppenolle of the Brussels region's Economics Ministry said on Monday.

Money transfer and messaging group Western Union, part of the family of payment instrument businesses owned by First Data Corp of the U.S., will open a call centre for Europe, Middle-East and North Africa before the end of 1997.

The operation will employ 200 people and will be located in the new "Triomphe" business centre. The total amount invested will be announced at a news conference by Brussels Economics Minister Jos Chabert on Wednesday, Van Coppenolle said.
The multilingual telephone centre, linked to the parent company in the U.S., will be used to receive orders and take customers calls from all over the world.
Van Copenolle said Sony was interested in setting up a assembly and distribution unit in Brussels. Negociations were still going on. An official decision was due in the next few months.
From Tokyo a Sony spokeswoman said the company could not confirm the plan.

Chabert's spokesman said, "The only thing I can confirm is talks are taking place for the opening of an assembly plant for mini-computers in or near Brussels. There is no date, we have not signed a thing yet." The plant would involve dozens of jobs.

He said Sony would also set up a call centre. It would rent offices and infrastructure in the Brussels' Brucall call centre hotel. From the centre Sony would provide customers with company information, take orders, conduct tele-marketing and so on.

Van Coppenolle said Western Union and Sony has chosen Brussels because of its role as Europe's capital, the availability of capable and multi-lingual staff and an attractive fiscal climate for foreign-owned operations.

For subsidiaries -- particularly those with services-related activities -- taxation is not linked to profits. Instead they are allowed more generous deductions of costs to ensure the functioning of the company such as telephone and electricity bills, rents, investment in software and so on.
